slides.title: Recapping Specification Standards and Use Case Modeling
bullets: Builds on standards for use case modeling covered in Week 4.
Formal specification standards prevent functional drift during automated code generation.
Establishes structured requirement engineering as the foundation for AI-assisted development.
slides.notes: Welcome back everyone. Last week, we examined international standards and specification guidelines for traditional use cases. Today, we step into Week 5 by connecting those specification principles directly to AI-driven software engineering. When using generative AI models or coding agents, weak requirements lead directly to incorrect implementations. We need rigorous specification standards to turn unstructured user requests into clean, machine-actionable boundaries.

slides.title: The Requirements Engineering Challenge in AI Coding
bullets: Unstructured product descriptions cause AI model hallucinations and scope creep.
Generative models require explicit boundaries to avoid generating unrequested assumptions.
Structured specifications serve as deterministic prompt anchors and validation criteria.
slides.notes: When stakeholders give us product ideas, they usually arrive as loose prose, informal emails, or incomplete user stories. If you feed unstructured text directly into an LLM coding agent, the agent fills in missing gaps with random assumptions. This introduces subtle bugs and architectural drift. Requirements engineering in the AI era is about transforming ambiguous language into unambiguous system constraints that anchor the AI's generation process.

slides.title: Fundamentals of Specification-Driven Development
bullets: Specification-Driven Development formalizes specifications before writing source code.
Specifications serve as the single source of truth for humans and AI agents.
Reduces downstream debugging by catching architectural ambiguity upfront.
slides.notes: Specification-Driven Development, or SDD, flips the traditional prompt-and-fix workflow. Instead of writing code directly or asking an AI to write code from a short prompt, SDD requires us to construct a rigorous specification document first. This document acts as a formal contract. Both human developers and automated coding agents treat this contract as the immutable specification baseline.

slides.title: Deconstructing Unstructured Product Descriptions
bullets: Identify hidden domain assumptions, passive verbs, and implicit requirements.
Extract core user intentions, system actors, and operational constraints systematically.
Categorize unstructured text into actors, triggers, preconditions, and postconditions.
slides.notes: To translate raw product text into specifications, we must systematically deconstruct narrative language. Look for passive phrasing like 'data is processed' and ask who or what processes it. Break down dense paragraphs into explicit actors, trigger events, strict preconditions, and verifiable postconditions. This structured decomposition removes ambiguity before any code generation tools are invoked.

slides.title: Establishing Clear System Boundaries
bullets: System boundaries define what the application handles versus external environments.
Explicit boundaries prevent AI agents from hallucinating external service implementations.
Categorize components as internal logic, external APIs, or explicit user touchpoints.
slides.notes: A critical step in requirements engineering is defining system boundaries. If an AI agent does not know where your software ends and an external API begins, it might generate redundant code or mock out infrastructure that already exists. This table illustrates how we explicitly separate internal system responsibilities from external integrations, providing clear targets for downstream development.

slides.title: Extracting Use Cases from Narrative Descriptions
bullets: Demonstrates converting a client feature request into formal use cases.
Identifies primary actors, functional goals, and clear system responses.
Transforms vague phrases like 'fast response' into quantifiable system boundaries.
slides.notes: Let's walk through an example. Suppose a client writes: 'Users should be able to upload invoices and get instant validation errors if formatting is wrong.' We extract the actor ('User'), the trigger ('Uploads invoice'), the boundary ('System validates format locally; does not process payments'), and the output ('Instant formatting error response'). Following this pipeline turns unstructured prose into precise use cases.

slides.title: Formulating Out-of-Scope Constraints
bullets: Explicitly listing out-of-scope items prevents feature creep and agent over-generation.
Defines system interfaces by specifying what the module will deliberately omit.
Establishes rigid architectural boundaries for generated software components.
slides.notes: Engineers often forget to define what a system should NOT do. When working with AI generators, unstated non-goals lead to bloat. If you specify an authentication service, explicitly state that user registration and password resets are out of scope if handled elsewhere. Out-of-scope boundaries keep generated code lean, modular, and strictly aligned with specified tasks.

slides.title: Concept Check: System Boundaries and Use Cases

quiz.question: When analyzing an unstructured client requirement for an AI-driven development pipeline, what is the primary purpose of defining explicit system boundaries?
options: To increase the context length needed by LLMs during generation.
To prevent AI agents from generating code for external or out-of-scope services.
To eliminate the need for writing unit tests after code is generated.
To automatically translate user interface designs into backend database schemas.
quiz.explanation: Defining clear system boundaries explicitly tells AI models what falls inside the module's scope and what relies on external dependencies. Option 1 is incorrect because boundaries reduce unnecessary context; Option 2 is correct; Option 3 is incorrect because tests are still needed; Option 4 is incorrect because boundaries define scope rather than direct UI translation.

slides.notes: Take a moment to answer this question. Think about how LLM coding agents behave when given ambiguous prompts with missing boundary constraints.

slides.title: Structuring Ambiguous Text into Formal Contracts
bullets: Convert prose into structured schemas like Gherkin, YAML, or JSON-spec.
Standardized schemas enforce consistent parsing by automated tools and agents.
Structured contracts support automated specification validation and test generation.
slides.notes: Once we extract use cases and system boundaries, we must format them into structured specifications. Informal text leads to varied interpretations. By standardizing our specs into formats like Gherkin syntax or structured YAML schemas, we create machine-readable contracts. These contracts can be validated for completeness before any code generation takes place.

slides.title: Managing Complexity Backpressure in Requirement Specs
bullets: Monolithic requirement documents cause performance decay in AI coding agents.
Partition specs into modular, hierarchically organized domain specifications.
Mitigates complexity backpressure across multi-step autonomous software tasks.
slides.notes: Research shows that AI coding performance drops significantly as task complexity and prompt size increase—a phenomenon known as complexity backpressure. If you feed an entire 50-page requirements document to an agent, accuracy plummets. Instead, engineering guidelines dictate decomposing requirements into small, self-contained sub-specifications focused on specific use cases.

slides.title: YAML Specification Artifact Walkthrough
bullets: Examines a structured YAML specification derived from unstructured product descriptions.
Demonstrates clear allocation of use cases, boundary inputs, and expected outcomes.
Serves as an input schema for spec-driven code generation frameworks.

figure.caption: Structured Specification Example
figure.code:
use_case:
  id: UC-01
  title: Process Invoice Upload
  actor: User
  boundary:
    in_scope: [Format Validation, Error Response]
    out_of_scope: [Payment Execution, Cloud Storage]
  preconditions:
    - User is authenticated
  scenario:
    given: A PDF file uploaded by the user
    when: File size is under 10MB
    then: Validate schema and return status code 200

slides.notes: Here is an example of a specification artifact written in YAML. Notice how clear and concise this is compared to a raw client paragraph. It explicitly lists the actor, the in-scope responsibilities, the out-of-scope boundaries, and a Gherkin-style test scenario. An AI agent reading this spec receives exact instructions without ambiguity.

slides.title: Concept Check: Specification-Driven Requirements

quiz.question: How does decomposing a large requirements document into modular specification artifacts mitigate 'complexity backpressure' in AI agents?
options: It increases the total number of lines of code generated per prompt.
It reduces cognitive load and prevents context window degradation in AI models.
It allows AI agents to bypass syntax checking during execution.
It guarantees that the generated code will run with zero latency.
quiz.explanation: Decomposing complex requirements into smaller, modular specs reduces the context volume and task complexity presented to an AI model at any single step. This prevents context window degradation and model confusion. Option 1 is wrong because line count isn't the goal; Option 2 is correct; Options 3 and 4 make false technical claims.

slides.notes: Consider how context window constraints and model attention mechanisms operate when answering this question.

slides.title: Preparing Specifications for Autonomous AI Agents
bullets: High-quality specifications enable autonomous agents to self-correct during generation.
Specifications feed directly into context protocols and test-generation pipelines.
Prepares specs for next class on executable specification frameworks.
slides.notes: Looking ahead, structured specifications are not just for generating implementation code; they also drive autonomous testing and verification. Agents use specs via context protocols (like MCP) to write test suites and verify their own output. When your specification clear defines boundaries and scenarios, autonomous agents can independently evaluate whether generated code meets requirements.

slides.title: Summary: Requirements Engineering for AI Systems
bullets: Unstructured descriptions must be systematically analyzed for actors and boundaries.
Specification-Driven Development treats formal specs as immutable contracts.
Modularizing specs mitigates complexity backpressure and prevents AI hallucination.
Next session: Connecting specification artifacts to spec-driven development frameworks.
slides.notes: To wrap up today's lecture: requirements engineering for AI software development requires transforming informal prose into structured, bounded specification artifacts. By defining clear system boundaries, explicitly listing out-of-scope items, and partitioning specs to avoid complexity backpressure, we set up AI agents for success. Next class, we will examine spec-driven development frameworks that turn these specs into executable code.
